content: Monitoring the health of individuals exposed to avian influenza, whether through infected birds or humans, is critical. Currently, avian influenza is not easily transmitted from animals to humans, and sustained human-to-human transmission has not been observed. However, it is essential to investigate suspected human cases to provide optimal treatment, identify other potential human contacts, monitor them for illness, and determine if human-to-human transmission is occurring. The primary goal of investigating human cases of avian influenza is to assess the extent of potential human-to-human transmission, particularly in clusters of cases and among contacts of confirmed cases. Health care facilities, including private clinicians, should be informed about the signs and symptoms of avian influenza in humans and the appropriate reporting channels for suspected cases. Any new suspected human case must be investigated, and confirmed cases should be reported to the World Health Organization (WHO) under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005). Enhanced surveillance should account for the health-seeking behavior of the population and may include active and passive approaches, both in health care settings and community-based monitoring. This includes monitoring individuals exposed to live or dead birds or animals. This allows for early detection of illness and timely initiation of antiviral treatment and isolation precautions. Individuals exposed to infected poultry or farms under suspicion should be closely monitored by local health authorities. Specimens must be packaged and transported safely to laboratories capable of confirming avian influenza infections. Sharing virus samples with WHO laboratories is encouraged to facilitate global monitoring and response. Preferred specimens include throat swabs for upper respiratory tract sampling, tracheal aspirates for intubated patients, and serum samples (acute and convalescent, if possible). Laboratories must be equipped to process and confirm avian influenza virus infections, and WHO can assist with sample shipment if needed. Proper specimen collection is vital for early case detection, patient management, and understanding the disease's epidemiology. It also aids in monitoring antiviral resistance, developing effective vaccines, and evaluating laboratory methods. Health care facilities must be prepared to manage patients with avian influenza. Standard and droplet precautions should be implemented, with airborne precautions applied during aerosol-generating procedures. Health care workers should be monitored for fever and influenza-like illness and provided with PPE and appropriate training. Case management should focus on preventing severe illness and death. Oseltamivir is the primary antiviral treatment, administered using the standard regimen for seasonal influenza. Modified regimens, such as higher dosages, longer durations, or combination therapy with amantadine or rimantadine, may be considered on a case-by-case basis. If in-country supplies of oseltamivir are insufficient, WHO can provide it from its global stockpile. Corticosteroids should not be used routinely but may be considered for septic shock with suspected adrenal insufficiency. Antibiotic chemoprophylaxis is not recommended, but antibiotics should be used to treat community-acquired pneumonia when present, guided by microbiological findings. Oxygen saturation should be monitored, and supplemental oxygen provided to correct hypoxemia. Therapy for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) associated with the A(H5N1) virus should follow evidence-based guidelines, including lung-protective mechanical ventilation strategies. Laboratory-confirmed cases must be reported to WHO under the IHR (2005). To gather more information on treatment and outcomes, treating physicians should complete and return clinical data reporting forms to WHO. Vaccination against influenza A(H5N1) is not widely available, and its use depends on the risk of infection. Vaccination is recommended for first responders to human or animal A(H5N1) outbreaks and health care workers managing suspected or confirmed cases in designated facilities. Seasonal influenza vaccines, while providing no protection against avian influenza, are recommended for health care workers in all countries to protect patients from seasonal influenza infections. Vaccines for human use against A(H5N1) have been developed and licensed in some countries but are not widely available. WHO does not maintain a stockpile of A(H5N1) vaccines. Pandemic influenza vaccine production can only begin once the pandemic virus is identified, with the first doses available four to six months after identification, given current vaccine technology. This document compiles information from WHO, FAO, and other UN agencies, as well as the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE), to provide guidance on avian influenza. It aims to assist WHO country offices and national institutions in advising Member States on human health concerns related to avian influenza outbreaks or suspected human infections. The document will be updated as new information becomes available.
